targets.from: judgement values, no photographs measured: a dense, spreading, clonal thicket much wider than tall (FEIS: often nearly impenetrable)

young.note: a low patch of a few shoots, or salal under a dense canopy

old.note: a tall, impenetrable thicket in a fog-belt opening or on a north-facing bluff

description: A thicket-forming evergreen shrub of the redwood forest and the foggy north-facing scrub, spreading by underground stems into dense patches. Its leaves are large, leathery and shiny, and its dark purple berries hang in rows below the leaves in late summer.

season_notes.winter: Leathery leaves stay green, some bronzing where the sun reaches them; deer browse it hard.
season_notes.spring: Bright new shoots and rows of white-pink urn flowers on reddish stalks.
season_notes.summer: Flowering ends and the hairy fruits swell and darken.
season_notes.fall: Dark blue-black berries hang along the stems into December.

range.where: Pacific coast from Alaska to the Santa Cruz Mountains, in redwood and mixed evergreen forest and on foggy bluffs and stabilised dunes; Marin, the Presidio and the Peninsula's north slopes

notes: Grown from coffeeberry (an evergreen broadleaf shrub with berries) as a lower, much wider, denser plant with more stems spread further, standing in for a rhizomatous clone that the generator cannot draw as one: a real patch is many joined shoots across several metres (FEIS). Leaves are 5-10 cm, thick, leathery, shiny dark green (FEIS), a little yellower and larger than evergreen huckleberry's, which it often grows beside. Flowers white to pink urns March-July in California, berries 6-10 mm, reddish to blue-black, August to October, staying to December. Deer use it heavily in winter (FEIS), and bears and birds eat the fruit; wrentits and band-tailed pigeons are named by FEIS but are not in the animal library. Heights: FEIS gives 0.4-3 m, tallest in the fog belt; around San Francisco it is mostly knee- to chest-high.
